PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 146 — Lesson 170: Medication Selection, Prescribing Safety & Monitoring Board Review

FNP-level goal: Choose an evidence-based medication only after confirming indication and patient fit, prescribe it accurately, anticipate interactions and life-stage risks, define monitoring and stopping rules, and evaluate whether the treatment produces meaningful benefit without unacceptable harm.

Learning Objectives

  • Use indication, treatment goal, evidence, contraindications, and patient preferences to select therapy.
  • Apply pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic principles to common board-style decisions.
  • Adjust prescribing reasoning for children, pregnancy, lactation, kidney or liver dysfunction, frailty, and older age.
  • Recognize major drug-drug, drug-disease, drug-food, and duplicate-ingredient risks.
  • Differentiate allergy, intolerance, predictable adverse effect, toxicity, and treatment failure.
  • Write a complete, unambiguous prescription and provide usable patient education.
  • Define baseline testing, follow-up interval, response target, toxicity monitoring, and stopping rules.
  • Practice antimicrobial, opioid, sedative, and polypharmacy stewardship.

Part 1 — Prescribing Is a Clinical Process

A prescription is not the end of diagnosis. It is a therapeutic trial with an indication, expected benefit, possible harm, monitoring plan, and decision point. The FNP remains responsible for confirming that the medicine is appropriate for this patient at this time.

Board-style questions may offer several drugs that treat the disease. The best answer is the one that fits severity, comorbidities, organ function, pregnancy potential, interactions, prior response, access, and the immediate clinical setting.

Part 2 — Begin With the Indication

State the diagnosis or justified working diagnosis, treatment goal, and whether medication is indicated. Some conditions require supportive care, observation, a procedure, emergency stabilization, or referral rather than a prescription.

Do not treat an abnormal number without understanding the syndrome. Do not start a familiar drug before excluding a contraindication or time-sensitive alternative diagnosis.

Part 3 — Define a Measurable Goal

The goal may be symptom relief, prevention of a complication, eradication of infection, reduction of exacerbations, improvement in function, or movement of a biomarker into an individualized range. Specify the expected time course.

A treatment cannot be evaluated if success was never defined. Patient-centered outcomes such as sleep, falls, pain interference, school or work function, and treatment burden may matter as much as a laboratory value.

Part 4 — Compare Benefit, Harm, and Burden

Consider absolute expected benefit, common adverse effects, rare serious risks, monitoring, administration complexity, interactions, cost, availability, route, frequency, and patient preference. More potent is not automatically better.

The safest effective option is often preferred, but undertreatment also causes harm. Balance disease risk against medication risk rather than focusing on only one side.

Part 5 — Read the Current Prescribing Information

FDA-approved prescribing information organizes indications, dosing, dosage forms, contraindications, warnings and precautions, adverse reactions, interactions, use in specific populations, and pharmacology. A boxed warning highlights serious risks that may lead to death or serious injury, but it does not automatically mean the medication can never be used.

Confirm the current label and authoritative clinical guideline. Drug information changes, and class memory may miss a product-specific warning, formulation, route, or interaction.

Part 6 — Pharmacokinetics: What the Body Does to the Drug

Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion shape drug exposure. Bioavailability, protein binding, volume of distribution, hepatic metabolism, renal elimination, and half-life affect onset, duration, loading, maintenance, and accumulation.

Steady state generally requires multiple half-lives. Changing a dose too quickly can lead to overcorrection before the full effect appears.

Part 7 — Pharmacodynamics: What the Drug Does to the Body

Pharmacodynamics includes receptor effects, dose-response, desired action, and toxicity. Greater exposure may improve effect until a ceiling is reached, while harm may continue to rise.

Older adults, patients with autonomic dysfunction, and people using multiple CNS-active agents can have amplified clinical responses even when measured drug concentrations appear ordinary.

Part 8 — Medication Reconciliation Before Selection

Reconcile prescription medicines, OTC products, vitamins, supplements, herbals, injections, inhalers, topicals, eye drops, PRN drugs, substances, and medicines obtained from other people or countries. Confirm what the patient actually takes, not only what appears in the EHR.

Ask the name, strength, route, frequency, indication, prescriber, adherence, benefit, adverse effects, and last dose. Duplicate therapy and duplicate active ingredients are common hidden hazards.

Part 9 — Clarify the Allergy Label

Record the suspected drug, reaction, timing, severity, treatment, re-exposure, and tolerance of related agents. Nausea from an antibiotic is not the same as anaphylaxis; a vague childhood rash is not the same as a severe cutaneous adverse reaction.

Do not delete a credible severe allergy, but do not allow an inaccurate label to force broader or more harmful therapy indefinitely. Refer for evaluation or delabeling when appropriate.

Part 10 — Contraindication, Warning, and Precaution

A contraindication identifies a situation in which the drug should not be used because risk is unacceptable. A warning or precaution calls attention to serious or clinically important risk and the conditions needed for safer use.

Board questions often hide the deciding fact in pregnancy status, severe kidney dysfunction, active bleeding, prolonged QT, asthma, bradycardia, drug interaction, or prior reaction.

Part 11 — Drug-Drug Interactions

Interactions may change absorption, metabolism, transport, elimination, receptor effect, or overlapping toxicity. Enzyme inhibition can raise exposure to a substrate; induction can reduce exposure, but direction and timing depend on the specific drugs.

Check a reliable interaction resource and the current label. Avoid relying only on memory, especially for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs, anticoagulants, antiarrhythmics, transplant medicines, seizure medicines, and complex antiviral therapy.

Part 12 — Drug-Disease and Drug-Food Interactions

A medicine can worsen an existing condition: a decongestant may aggravate hypertension, an anticholinergic may worsen retention or confusion, an NSAID may worsen kidney disease, edema, bleeding, or heart failure, and a sedative may worsen falls or sleep-disordered breathing.

Food, alcohol, supplements, and minerals can alter absorption or toxicity. Ask specifically rather than assuming nonprescription products are harmless.

Part 13 — Kidney Function and Dosing

Determine whether the drug or active metabolite is renally cleared, which kidney estimate the dosing guidance uses, whether a loading dose differs from maintenance, and how rapidly kidney function is changing. eGFR and creatinine clearance are not interchangeable for every label.

Acute kidney injury makes steady-state estimates unreliable. Reduce, extend the interval, choose an alternative, or monitor concentrations as appropriate. Also consider whether the drug itself can worsen kidney function, potassium, volume, or acid-base balance.

Part 14 — Liver Disease and Prescribing

Serum aminotransferases do not directly measure metabolic capacity. Consider synthetic function, bilirubin, portal hypertension, decompensation, interacting drugs, alcohol, nutrition, and the product's hepatic guidance.

Avoid simplistic rules such as cutting every dose in half. Some medications require avoidance, some careful titration, and others little change. Suspected drug-induced liver injury requires evaluation of timing, competing causes, severity, and prompt discontinuation when appropriate.

Part 15 — Pediatric Prescribing

Verify current weight in kilograms, indication, age restrictions, formulation concentration, dose per kilogram, frequency, maximum dose, renal or hepatic considerations, and caregiver ability to measure and administer. Never convert pounds incorrectly or omit the maximum adult-equivalent limit when applicable.

Write the concentration and volume clearly for liquids. Demonstrate the dosing device and use teach-back. A decimal error can produce a tenfold overdose: use a leading zero for values below one and avoid trailing zeros.

Part 16 — Pregnancy and Reproductive Potential

Ask about pregnancy, possibility of conception, reproductive goals, contraception when relevant, and urgency of treatment. Compare maternal disease risk, fetal or neonatal risk, gestational timing, dose, alternatives, and evidence.

FDA's Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule replaced the old letter categories with narrative risk information. Do not use obsolete A-B-C-D-X shorthand as the sole basis for a decision. Some medicines require a pregnancy test, contraception, washout, or specialist coordination.

Part 17 — Lactation

Consider milk transfer, oral bioavailability to the infant, infant age and prematurity, dose timing, maternal indication, duration, and potential effect on milk production. A safe maternal dose is not automatically safe for every breastfeeding infant.

Use reliable lactation-specific information and counsel on infant monitoring. Avoid unnecessarily stopping breastfeeding or withholding effective maternal therapy when compatible alternatives exist.

Part 18 — Older Adults and Frailty

Age-related changes in kidney function, body composition, homeostasis, cognition, vision, dexterity, and drug sensitivity increase risk. Frailty, falls, orthostasis, constipation, retention, delirium, and treatment burden should influence selection and targets.

The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria identifies potentially inappropriate medicines, drug-disease interactions, drug-drug interactions, cautions, and renal adjustments. It supports but does not replace individualized shared decision-making, and it is not intended as an automatic denial list.

Part 19 — Anticholinergic and Sedative Burden

Multiple individually modest agents can create cumulative dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, cognitive impairment, falls, or sedation. OTC sleep and allergy products are frequent contributors.

Count burden across the entire regimen. Before adding a medicine for a new symptom, ask whether the symptom is an adverse effect of an existing drug.

Part 20 — QT and Arrhythmia Risk

Risk rises with multiple QT-prolonging drugs, congenital long-QT syndrome, bradycardia, structural heart disease, female sex-related biology, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and high exposure from interactions or organ dysfunction.

Use current drug-specific guidance, correct electrolytes, avoid unnecessary combinations, and obtain ECG monitoring when indicated. Syncope or palpitations in a high-risk medication context may require urgent evaluation.

Part 21 — Serotonergic and Sympathomimetic Toxicity

Combining serotonergic agents can cause mental-status change, autonomic instability, neuromuscular hyperactivity, and hyperthermia. Sympathomimetics can increase heart rate, blood pressure, anxiety, and ischemic risk.

Review antidepressants, migraine treatments, stimulants, decongestants, pain medicines, supplements, and recent changes. Severe toxicity is an emergency, not a routine medication-adjustment visit.

Part 22 — Bleeding Risk and Antithrombotic Therapy

Assess indication, dose, kidney or liver function, age, weight when label-relevant, prior bleeding, anemia, platelets, falls context, interacting antiplatelets, NSAIDs, alcohol, and procedural plans. Do not stop a necessary anticoagulant reflexively for minor bruising, but do not ignore significant bleeding.

Know when urgent reversal, emergency transfer, specialist coordination, or temporary interruption is indicated. Medication reconciliation at transitions is essential.

Part 23 — Antimicrobial Stewardship

Confirm a bacterial syndrome and whether antibiotics improve outcomes. Select the narrowest effective agent using site, likely organism, allergies, local resistance, culture data, organ function, pregnancy, interactions, and disease severity.

Use the correct dose and shortest evidence-supported duration. Provide symptom care and return precautions when antibiotics are not indicated. CDC describes outpatient stewardship through commitment, action, tracking and reporting, and education and expertise.

Part 24 — Controlled Substances and Opioid Safety

Confirm indication, expected functional benefit, alternatives, substance-use and overdose risk, mental health, respiratory disease, concurrent sedatives, prescription-monitoring data, toxicology when appropriate, consent, secure storage, and follow-up.

Avoid automatic escalation for persistent pain without reassessment. Provide naloxone when risk warrants and follow federal, state, and institutional requirements. Acute overdose, severe sedation, or respiratory depression requires emergency response.

Part 25 — Start Low Is Not the Whole Plan

Starting conservatively may reduce harm in frailty or sensitivity, but underdosing can leave dangerous disease untreated. Select a rational initial dose, then define titration steps, maximum, target, monitoring, and when to stop.

Do not titrate faster than the pharmacology and clinical outcome allow. Conversely, do not leave an ineffective starter dose unchanged for months.

Part 26 — Baseline Monitoring

Before prescribing, identify what must be known: vital signs, pregnancy status, kidney or liver function, electrolytes, ECG, blood count, infection testing, mood or suicide risk, weight, drug level, or another measure depending on the therapy.

Order only what is clinically indicated, but do not omit a safety-critical baseline. Document how results affect the plan.

Part 27 — Follow-Up Monitoring

Set a time to assess adherence, benefit, adverse effects, vital signs, function, laboratory results, and patient priorities. The interval should match disease severity, drug onset, half-life, titration, and risk.

Define what constitutes adequate response, partial response, treatment failure, toxicity, and need for referral. A refill without evaluation is not always safe continuation.

Part 28 — Side Effect, Allergy, Toxicity, or Disease?

A predictable dose-related adverse effect may improve with dose change or time. Immune-mediated allergy can require avoidance and documentation. Toxicity may reflect excess exposure, interaction, organ failure, or overdose. New disease may be mistakenly blamed on a medication.

Characterize timing, dose relationship, objective findings, dechallenge, rechallenge risk, and alternative causes before labeling the event.

Part 29 — Adherence Is a Diagnostic Question

Ask neutrally how many doses were missed, how the medicine is taken, cost, access, beliefs, side effects, literacy, routine, caregiving, dexterity, and pharmacy barriers. Apparent treatment resistance may be nonuse, incorrect technique, or inability to obtain the medicine.

Simplify regimens, align timing, use affordable alternatives, teach inhaler or injection technique, engage pharmacists, and confirm understanding. Avoid blaming the patient for a system problem.

Part 30 — Deprescribing

Each medicine needs a current indication. Identify therapeutic duplication, prescribing cascades, no-benefit therapy, goals that have changed, excessive burden, high-risk combinations, and drugs continued past their intended duration.

Prioritize with the patient, assess withdrawal or rebound risk, taper when required, monitor what returns, and document who follows the change. Deprescribing is active care, not abandonment.

Part 31 — Write an Unambiguous Prescription

Include patient, date, generic drug and formulation, strength, route, dose, frequency, duration or quantity, indication when helpful, refills, and required legal elements. Avoid unsafe abbreviations, vague ranges, unclear PRN indications, and conflicting instructions.

For devices and liquids, specify concentration, dose volume, supplies, and technique. Confirm the pharmacy and reconcile what was actually dispensed.

Part 32 — Patient Education and Teach-Back

Explain purpose, how and when to take it, expected benefit, common effects, serious warning symptoms, interactions, missed-dose plan, monitoring, duration, storage, and when to contact the clinic or seek emergency care.

Use plain language, interpreter services, written instructions, and teach-back. The label may be accurate but still unusable to a patient with limited vision, literacy, English proficiency, or dexterity.

Part 33 — Medication Errors and Transitions

Hospital discharge, specialist visits, pharmacy substitutions, formulary changes, and care-setting transitions create omission, duplication, and dose-conflict risk. Compare the pre-transition list, discharge list, and what the patient is taking.

Resolve discrepancies, communicate changes to the full team, discontinue obsolete orders when possible, and arrange laboratory and clinical follow-up.

Part 34 — Common Board-Style Prescribing Traps

  • Choosing a drug before confirming indication
  • Ignoring pregnancy, allergy, kidney function, or a serious interaction
  • Selecting a class-correct drug with the wrong route or formulation
  • Confusing a boxed warning with an absolute contraindication
  • Treating a viral syndrome with an antibiotic
  • Adding medication to treat another medication's adverse effect
  • Using a potentially inappropriate geriatric medicine without considering alternatives
  • Failing to define monitoring, follow-up, or stopping rules
  • Escalating therapy before assessing adherence and technique

Clinical Case 1 — The Hidden OTC Interaction

An older adult with hypertension, urinary retention, and recent falls requests a nighttime product for allergies and sleep. The product contains a sedating first-generation antihistamine.

Reasoning: The medication can add anticholinergic and sedative burden, worsen retention, cognition, orthostasis, and falls. Clarify the symptom, review the entire regimen, use nonpharmacologic measures or safer targeted alternatives, and avoid treating the brand name rather than its active ingredients.

Clinical Case 2 — The Kidney Function Trap

A patient with acute dehydration and rapidly rising creatinine is prescribed a renally eliminated medicine using an automated dose based on the current eGFR.

Reasoning: Kidney function is not at steady state, so the estimate may be unreliable. Reassess urgency and indication, restore perfusion when appropriate, use drug-specific guidance, consider holding or selecting an alternative, and monitor closely.

Clinical Case 3 — Apparent Resistant Asthma

A patient remains symptomatic despite escalating inhalers. Before another medicine is added, observation shows incorrect inhaler technique and the patient reports skipping doses because of cost.

Reasoning: This is not yet proven pharmacologic failure. Correct technique, address access, confirm diagnosis and triggers, then reassess before escalating treatment and adverse-effect burden.

Clinical Case 4 — Prescribing Cascade

An older adult develops ankle edema after a medication change. A diuretic is added, followed by potassium replacement and treatment for dizziness.

Reasoning: Reconstruct the timeline and ask whether the first medicine caused edema. Adjusting or replacing the offending drug may remove several downstream prescriptions and reduce falls and electrolyte risk.

FNP High-Yield Framework: SAFER Rx

  1. S — State the indication and stability: Diagnosis, severity, emergency needs, and measurable goal.
  2. A — Assess patient fit: Allergies, age, pregnancy, organ function, comorbidities, prior response, preferences, and access.
  3. F — Find the best evidence and formulation: Current guideline, label, route, dose, frequency, duration, and alternatives.
  4. E — Examine interactions and errors: Full reconciliation, duplication, drug-drug, drug-disease, OTC, supplements, and calculation.
  5. R — Review monitoring and response: Baseline, follow-up, benefit, toxicity, adherence, titration, and stopping rules.
  6. Rx — Communicate and close the prescription loop: Clear order, education, teach-back, pharmacy confirmation, documentation, and transition safety.

Take-Home Summary

Safe prescribing begins with a justified indication, patient stability, and a measurable goal. Compare benefit, harm, burden, evidence, formulation, and access. Reconcile every prescription, OTC product, supplement, and actual use; clarify allergies; check contraindications, interactions, duplicate ingredients, and the current FDA label. Apply pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic principles while adapting to pediatrics, pregnancy, lactation, kidney or liver dysfunction, older age, and frailty. Consider cumulative anticholinergic, sedative, QT, serotonergic, bleeding, and organ-toxicity risk. Practice antimicrobial and controlled-substance stewardship. Write an unambiguous prescription, teach the patient how to use it, define baseline and follow-up monitoring, evaluate adherence before escalation, and deprescribe when benefit no longer exceeds harm. A medication remains appropriate only when indication, benefit, safety, and patient goals remain aligned.

Educational note: This lesson is educational and does not replace current FDA-approved prescribing information, federal or state prescribing law, controlled-substance requirements, clinical guidelines, pharmacy consultation, individualized care, or emergency management. Drug indications, warnings, formulations, interactions, and recommendations change. Verify current authoritative drug information and patient-specific factors before clinical use.
